extracted.intended_audience: government attorneys, judge advocate staff, disbursing officers, and federal officials handling public property and public funds
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and administrative standards governing disposition, custody, accounting, and jurisdiction over United States public money and public property, especially as applied to military and disbursing officers. Covers statutory constraints, courtroom/procedural requirements, accounting rules, and distinctions between licenses and grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: No privity between Government and subcontractor
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no privity of contract between the Government and a subcontractor, and he has no legal claim whatever upon the United States for any part of the contract money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcontractors must look to the principal contractor for payment; government is not directly liable to subcontractors (cases cited: R. 52, 194, May 19, 1887; C. 746, Dec. 13, 1894).

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts cannot enjoin federal judiciary or officers
rubrics_metrics.description: A State court can have no authority to enjoin the United States judiciary from executing their judgments, or from proceeding with actions of law pending before them; similarly a State court was not empowered to enjoin an executive department or officer of the United States from performing the contracts of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An injunction issued in a State court prohibiting an Army officer charged with paying a contractor from paying said sum would legally and properly be disregarded by such officer (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements for suits against the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: When suit is initiated against the United States the plaintiff is required to proceed according to the provisions of secs. 4, 5, and 6 of the act of Mar. 3, 1887 (24 Stat. 506), and must duly serve a copy of the petition upon the proper United States district attorney and mail a copy to the Attorney General.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to follow this procedure may be fatal to the suit (not followed in the cited case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbursing officer's authority to pursue legal remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: It is accordance with military usage and general practice that an officer of the Army charged with disbursement of public funds may pursue in his own name and representative capacity the proper legal remedies when such funds are illegally appropriated or withheld by third parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duty should not be imposed on the head of the department; the disbursing officer should file and prove claims (e.g., in bankruptcy) and prosecute collection with due and reasonable diligence to support future applications to be discharged from liability for losses resulting from depository failure (R.35,365, May 7, 1874).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for bank exchange charges not deductible by officer
rubrics_metrics.description: A disbursing officer who deposited in a bank for collection a check drawn on the treasurer of the Philippine Islands and was charged exchange by the bank is not entitled to take credit in his account for the sum required to be paid as exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bank charged $30.11 as exchange; officer could not credit that amount in official accounts (C. 18853, Aug. 21, 1907).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3620 R.S. — drawing only in favor of payees
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3620, R.S., provides that a disbursing officer having public moneys on deposit in a public depository shall draw for the same only in favor of the persons to whom payment is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment by a disbursing officer to a firm on the order of a party indebted to the United States was held to be in contravention of the statute (P. 53, 239, Apr. 29, 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 1766 R.S. applies to bonded disbursing officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1766, R.S., though expressed in somewhat general terms, properly applied only to bonded disbursing officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction of the provision limits its operation to those officers who are bonded (P. 61, 167, Aug. 22, 1893).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's authority re disbursing agents for appropriations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Congress appropriates money to be expended under the direction of the Secretary of War, the Secretary is authorized to commit disbursement to any proper person, and should properly designate the engineer officer engaged in superintending the work as disbursing agent so the duty is performed without charge to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to new State, War, and Navy Building appropriations (R. 41,283, June 22, 1878).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for forged/altered checks — bank bears loss absent neglect
rubrics_metrics.description: When a paymaster's check was indorsed in blank by payee and the paymaster subindorsed only for identification, and the check was later materially altered and paid by the Assistant Treasurer, the loss fell upon the assistant treasurer whose liability is the same as that of a bank which pays a forged check, provided the forgery was not facilitated by the drawer's negligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parol evidence to show that the paymaster indorsed merely for identification would not be admissible in the hands of a bona fide indorsee (P. 53, 312, May, 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection act (Apr. 20, 1874) limited to appropriations by Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of April 20, 1874, entitled 'An act to provide for the inspection of the disbursements of appropriations made by officers of the Army' applied only to disbursements of moneys appropriated by legislation of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope limitation clarified by opinion (P. 148, 184, July 9, 1891).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3651 R.S. — prohibition on exchange with limited exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3651, R.S., prohibits the exchange of funds by any disbursing officer or agent of the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, exchanging Army pay funds for Philippine currency at market rate to enable payment in that currency to creditors desiring it was held not to be an exchange forbidden by the section (C. 17604, Feb. 28, 1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounts and receipts must be in US currency, subject to creditor consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Under sections 3473–3476 and 3617–3692 R.S., funds received by disbursing officers from sale of stores and other public property must be in United States currency and accounts of disbursing officers must be kept in United States currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonetheless, there is no objection to payment of a debt of the United States in any local currency which the creditor is willing to receive; contracts payable in foreign currency are permitted but accounts must be stated in US legal tender at the market quotation on day of payment (C. 15316, Dec. 23, 1903).

rubrics_metrics.name: Damage to public property — deduction from pay vs voluntary payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Regulations paragraph 687 provided that damage to public property for which an officer was responsible would be deducted from his monthly pay; the regulation was intended to cover cases where the officer did not voluntarily pay the amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the officer is willing to pay the amount voluntarily, it should be received from him and deposited to the credit of miscellaneous receipts, and the officer relieved from his accountability (C. 22134, Oct. 1, 1907).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections 3617 and 3618 apply only after money received for US use
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 3617 and 3618, R.S., have no application until the money has been received to the use of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accordingly, contractual provisions (e.g., lease allowing lessee to make repairs and have cost credited on rent) were held lawful; similarly, a contract for laundry services in exchange for fuel and water at cost price was lawful (C. 29129, Oct. 18, 1911; C. 14948, July 15, 1903).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of public property requires Congressional authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: The disposition (sale, grant, transfer, or other grant of interest) of public property must be authorized by Congress; neither executive departments nor military officers may convey interests in land or other public property without statutory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule applies to both personal and real property and to exchanges; authority must be clear and express (numerous opinions and cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between license and grant/ususfructuary interest
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear distinction exists between a grant of a usufructuary interest in land and a revocable license; a license that is revocable and does not transfer a permanent interest may be permissible without Congressional conveyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Secretary may permit telegraph posts removable at gov't will or license a post trader to erect necessary buildings; but cannot grant permanent franchises or exclusive usufructuary interests such as indefinite hotels or toll-charging ferries on military reservations (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to condemn/purchase land must be express and precede suit
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to condemn (eminent domain) or purchase land for the United States must be express in statute and must precede the institution of suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory authority for purchase must be clear; 'purchase' includes donations, and appropriations alone may be insufficient; title must be approved by the Attorney General with abstracts, surveys, and certificates as to liens (see Section 3736 discussions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title approval and related requirements for land acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: Title for land acquired for the United States must be approved by the Attorney General and supported by abstract of title, survey, and certificate as to liens; special rules apply for limited uses, condition subsequent, easements, deposits in condemnation, vesting, and errors as to area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific checks (abstracts, surveys, lien certificates) are required to validate title; various limited-use and conditional title scenarios described (pages cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: No adverse possession against the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: No title can be acquired by adverse possession against the United States; US possession is protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process for protecting US title and possession discussed; statutory and case authority cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability for public property and procedures to fix or relieve it
rubrics_metrics.description: Accountability for public property is subject to procedures: responsibility for transportation requests, liability for loss as gratuitous bailee, fixing accountability by surveying officer (including swearing of officer and witnesses), receipt of affidavits, and relief from accountability under appropriate conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveying officers have roles in fixing accountability; relief requires due process and proof; various procedural details are laid out (pages referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Military reservations: acquisition, limits, and disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Military reservations can be created by authority of the President or Congress, are not subject to private location for mines or to State authorization of rights of way, and disposition (including sale or grants) of reservation lands requires Congressional authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reservations may be in territories, national parks, or islands; conflicting private claims, sales under special acts, and rights (e.g., boundaries, easements) are governed by statute and precedent (pages 922–927 and following).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of way over public property require Congressional authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A State cannot authorize rights of way over public property; authority of Congress is required for rights of way of the United States under grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal acceptance may not be necessary in every case, but location selection, joint use requirements, and special statutory grants govern (pages 944–946).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sales of military stores — condemnation and manner of sale
rubrics_metrics.description: Military stores under section 1241, Revised Statutes, must be condemned as damaged or unsuitable before sale; the statute defines 'military stores' and prescribes manner and terms of sale (including use of auctioneers, credit sales in some cases, and restrictions on exchanges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of 'unsuitable' property given (not adapted for use, by reason of situation, matured/fallen timber, etc.); disposition of proceeds governed by section 3618 (pages 958–960).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional grant — Article IV sec. 3 para. 2 (Congressional power)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution grants Congress power to dispose of and make all needful rules and regulations respecting territory or other property belonging to the United States; this is comprehensive and prevents executive conveyance without Congressional authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Executive officers, including the Secretary of War or heads of departments, cannot alienate US land or convey interests except pursuant to express or implied acts of Congress; later statutes (e.g., act of July 28, 1892) may modify specific authorities (e.g., short-term revocable leases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounts and payments in local currency — creditor consent rule
rubrics_metrics.description: While accounts of disbursing officers must be kept in United States currency, the United States may pay its debts in local currency if the creditor is willing to receive payment in that currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: employees employed at a rate in dollars are entitled to demand US currency, but may accept foreign currency equal in value on payment day; contracts payable in foreign currency are permissible provided accounts are stated in US legal tender at market quotation (C. 15316, Dec. 23, 1903).
